problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have completed a fully rigorous solution. The minimum number of tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{2025}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Structure of the uncovered squares.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a *permutation matrix*: there exists a bijection \(\sigma:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (with \(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered squares are precisely \((i,\sigma(i))\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n\).

2. **Upper bound – explicit construction with \(n\) tiles.**  
   For every row \(i\) place a horizontal \(1\times (n-1)\) tile covering all squares of that row except the uncovered one \((i,\sigma(i))\).  
   The \(n\) tiles are pairwise disjoint and together cover every square that is not uncovered, showing that \(n\) tiles are sufficient.

3. **Lower bound – a rank argument.**  
   *Encoding.*  Let \(M\) be the \(n\times n\) \(\{0,1\}\)-matrix whose entry \(M_{ij}=1\) iff the square \((i,j)\) is covered and \(0\) otherwise.  
   Then \(M = J-P_\sigma\), where \(J\) is the all‑ones matrix and \(P_\sigma\) is the permutation matrix of \(\sigma\).

   *Each tile is rank 1.*  A rectangular tile occupies a set of rows \(R\) and a set of columns \(C\); its indicator matrix equals \(u v^{\mathsf T}\) with  
   \[
   u_i=\begin{cases}1,&i\in R,\\0,&i\notin R,\end{cases}\qquad
   v_j=\begin{cases}1,&j\in C,\\0,&j\notin C,\end{cases}
   \]
   which has rank 1 over \(\mathbb R\).

   *Summation of tiles.*  If \(t\) tiles are used, the covering matrix is the sum of their indicator matrices:
   \[
   M=\sum_{k=1}^{t}u^{(k)}\bigl(v^{(k)}\bigr)^{\mathsf T}.
   \]
   Since \(\operatorname{rank}(A+B)\le\operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{rank}(B)\), we obtain
   \[
   \operatorname{rank}(M)\le\sum_{k=1}^{t}1 = t.
   \tag{1}
   \]

   *Computing \(\operatorname{rank}(M)\).*  Permuting rows and columns does not change rank.  Multiplying \(M\) on the left by the permutation matrix \(P_\sigma^{\mathsf T}\) yields
   \[
   P_\sigma^{\mathsf T}M = P_\sigma^{\mathsf T}J - I = J - I,
   \]
   because \(P_\sigma^{\mathsf T}J=J\).  Hence \(\operatorname{rank}(M)=\operatorname{rank}(J-I)\).

   To find \(\operatorname{rank}(J-I)\), solve \((J-I)x=0\):
   \[
   (J-I)x = (\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}x)\,\mathbf 1 - x = 0
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   x = (\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}x)\,\mathbf 1.
   \]
   Thus every component of \(x\) equals the same scalar \(c=\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}x\).  Substituting gives \(c = n c\), i.e. \((n-1)c=0\).  Since \(n>1\), we obtain \(c=0\) and consequently \(x=0\).  Therefore \(J-I\) is invertible, so
   \[
   \operatorname{rank}(J-I)=n.
   \]

   *Conclusion of the lower bound.*  From (1) we have \(t\ge\operatorname{rank}(M)=n\).  Thus any admissible placement uses at least \(n=2025\) tiles.

4. **Matching bounds.**  The construction uses exactly \(n\) tiles, and the rank argument shows that fewer than \(n\) tiles are impossible.  Hence the minimum number of tiles is \(n=2025\).

---

### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  Index the rows and columns of the grid by \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).

#### 1.  The uncovered squares form a permutation matrix  

Because each row contains exactly one uncovered unit square, there exists a function
\[
\sigma:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]
such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) lies in column \(\sigma(i)\).  
Since each column also contains exactly one uncovered square, \(\sigma\) is bijective; hence it is a permutation.  
Consequently the set of uncovered squares is
\[
U=\{(i,\sigma(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\},
\]
the positions of the \(1\)’s of the permutation matrix \(P_\sigma\).

#### 2.  Upper bound: a covering with \(n\) tiles  

For each row \(i\) place the horizontal rectangle
\[
R_i=\{i\}\times\bigl(\{1,\dots ,n\}\setminus\{\sigma(i)\}\bigr).
\]
\(R_i\) is a \(1\times (n-1)\) tile whose sides lie on grid lines.  It covers precisely those squares of row \(i\) that are not in \(U\).  
The rows are distinct, so the rectangles \(R_1,\dots ,R_n\) are pairwise disjoint.  Every square that is not uncovered belongs to exactly one of the \(R_i\).  Hence \(n\) tiles suffice:
\[
\text{minimum number of tiles}\le n=2025.
\]

#### 3.  Lower bound via matrix rank  

Define the covering matrix \(M=(m_{ij})\) by
\[
m_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if the square }(i,j)\text{ is covered},\\[2pt]
0 & \text{if the square }(i,j)\text{ is uncovered}.
\end{cases}
\]
All uncovered squares are exactly those of \(P_\sigma\); therefore
\[
M = J - P_\sigma,
\]
where \(J\) denotes the \(n\times n\) all‑ones matrix.

##### 3.1  Indicator matrix of a tile  

A rectangular tile occupies a non‑empty set of rows \(R\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) and a non‑empty set of columns \(C\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that no uncovered square lies inside the rectangle (i.e. \(\sigma(R)\cap C=\varnothing\)).  
Its indicator matrix is
\[
U_{RC}=u v^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
u_i=
\begin{cases}
1 & i\in R,\\
0 & i\notin R,
\end{cases}
\qquad
v_j=
\begin{cases}
1 & j\in C,\\
0 & j\notin C.
\end{cases}
\]
Since \(u\neq0\) and \(v\neq0\), \(\operatorname{rank}(U_{RC})=1\).

##### 3.2  Summation of tiles  

Assume a placement uses \(t\) tiles, with indicator matrices \(U_1,\dots ,U_t\).  
Because the tiles are disjoint (no unit square is covered twice), the covering matrix is the sum of these indicator matrices:
\[
M = \sum_{k=1}^{t} U_k.
\]
For any matrices \(A,B\) we have \(\operatorname{rank}(A+B)\le\operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{rank}(B)\).  Applying this repeatedly yields
\[
\operatorname{rank}(M)\le\sum_{k=1}^{t}\operatorname{rank}(U_k)
= \sum_{k=1}^{t}1 = t.
\tag{2}
\]

##### 3.3  Computing \(\operatorname{rank}(M)\)  

Row and column permutations are performed by multiplication with permutation matrices, which are invertible; thus they preserve rank.  Multiply \(M\) on the left by \(P_\sigma^{\mathsf T}\) (the inverse of \(P_\sigma\)):
\[
P_\sigma^{\mathsf T}M = P_\sigma^{\mathsf T}J - I.
\]
Since each row of \(J\) consists entirely of ones, left‑multiplication by any permutation matrix leaves \(J\) unchanged: \(P_\sigma^{\mathsf T}J = J\).  Hence
\[
P_\sigma^{\mathsf T}M = J - I.
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{rank}(M)=\operatorname{rank}(J-I).
\]

To determine \(\operatorname{rank}(J-I)\), solve \((J-I)x=0\) for \(x\in\mathbb R^{n}\):
\[
(J-I)x = (\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}x)\,\mathbf 1 - x = 0,
\]
where \(\mathbf 1\) denotes the all‑ones column vector.  The equation implies \(x = (\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}x)\,\mathbf 1\); thus every component of \(x\) equals the same scalar \(c=\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}x\).  Substituting back gives \(c = n c\), i.e. \((n-1)c=0\).  Since \(n>1\), we obtain \(c=0\) and consequently \(x=0\).  Hence the only solution is the zero vector, so \(J-I\) is invertible.  Consequently
\[
\operatorname{rank}(J-I)=n.
\]

Thus \(\operatorname{rank}(M)=n\).

##### 3.4  Consequence  

From (2) we obtain
\[
t \ge \operatorname{rank}(M)=n.
\]
Therefore any admissible placement must use at least \(n=2025\) tiles.

#### 4.  Conclusion  

We have exhibited a placement using exactly \(2025\) tiles and proved that no placement can use fewer.  Hence the minimal possible number of tiles is

\[
\boxed{2025}.
\]
